title: The Journey to Ta'if
subtitle: Rejection in the Mountains and the Mercy of the Messenger
summary: The arduous sixty-mile trek to the mountain city of Ta'if, the cold scorn of the chieftains of Thaqif, the pelting, the orchard, and Addas as sirah, and, separately, the Angel of the Mountains at Qarn al-Tha'alib in Bukhari and Muslim.

sections.text: Seeking Haven in the High Country

In the month of Shawwal of the tenth year of Prophethood, with Makkah engulfed in hostility following the deaths of Abu Talib and Khadijah, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ set his sights toward the mountain city of Ta'if. Situated approximately sixty miles southeast of Makkah amid the rugged peaks of the Sarawat range, Ta'if was the fertile summer resort of the Hijaz, governed by the powerful tribe of Banu Thaqif. The Prophet hoped they might grant him sanctuary, embrace monotheism, and provide a secure base from which the divine message could spread unhindered.

Refusing to ride, the Prophet ﷺ undertook the steep, rock-strewn journey on foot across scorching plains and steep ascents, accompanied solely by his devoted freedman and adopted son, Zayd ibn Harithah. Traveling without an armed escort or tribal banner, the two walked with quiet resolve, motivated entirely by faith and pastoral dedication to their sacred trust.
The steep mountain passes of the Sarawat range along the arduous ascent toward Ta'if.
The Arrogance of Thaqif's Chieftains

Upon reaching Ta'if, the Prophet ﷺ went directly to the grand estate of the city's three paramount chieftains—three chiefs whom the sirah names as Abd Yalil, Mas'ud, and Habib. The hadith of the Angel of the Mountains, which is a separate report, names the refusal of Ibn Abd Yalil. Sitting before them with dignity, he invited them to the worship of the One God and asked them to assist him in delivering his message to mankind.

Their response was steeped in venomous arrogance and derisive contempt. One brother mocked: 'Could God find no one better to send as a prophet than you?' The second jeered: 'He would tear the curtains of the Kaaba if God had truly sent you!' The third scoffed: 'By God, I will never speak to you! If you are indeed a messenger from God as you claim, your status is too perilous for me to converse with; and if you are lying about God, you are too lowly for me to address.' Stung by their cruelty, the Prophet ﷺ requested that they at least keep his visit secret so as not to incite Quraysh further against him, but they refused even this basic courtesy.
The Ordeal Along the Orchard Road

The stoning that follows is the narrative in Ibn Hisham, not the text of Bukhari 3231 or Muslim 1795. In that account the chieftains incited the town's rowdiest youths, slaves, and idle crowds to harass him. They formed two parallel lines along the narrow road leading out of the city, armed with sharp stones and rocks. As the Prophet ﷺ and Zayd walked through the gauntlet, the mob hurled insults and pelted them with stones.

Zayd threw himself in front of the Messenger of God, attempting to shield him with his own body, and sustained severe head wounds. The barrage continued relentlessly until the Prophet's feet and ankles were severely bruised and lacerated, his blood soaking into his sandals. Whenever he stumbled from pain, the crowd forced him to his feet with jeers only to resume stoning him, driving the two exhausted travelers nearly three miles beyond the outskirts of the town.
The solitary vineyard landscapes where the wounded Messenger sought shelter and poured out his supplication.
Shelter in the Vineyard and the Servant Addas

The vineyard of Utbah and Shaybah, the servant Addas, and the supplication under the vine are likewise the sirah of Ibn Hisham. They are not part of the hadith of the Angel of the Mountains. In that account the two men took shelter in the orchard, and the Prophet turned to God. The supplication is transmitted at length in the sirah. This chapter quotes only the opening, and does not treat the longer wording as a numbered hadith.

اللَّهُمَّ إِلَيْكَ أَشْكُو ضَعْفَ قُوَّتِي، وَقِلَّةَ حِيلَتِي، وَهَوَانِي عَلَى النَّاسِ
'O God, to You I complain of the weakness of my strength, the scantness of my means, and my being of little account among people.' — opening of the supplication in the sirah of Ibn Hisham. The longer form, in that same account, asks God not to leave him to a distant stranger or an enemy, and says that if God is not displeased with him he does not mind. It is not quoted here in full.

Watching from a distance, Utbah and Shaybah felt a stir of tribal pity for their kinsman. They called their Christian servant, a young man from Nineveh named Addas, and instructed him to take a platter of grapes to the wounded traveler. When Addas presented the fruit, the Prophet reached his hand forward and uttered: 'Bismillah' (In the Name of God), before eating.

Addas looked up in astonishment and remarked: 'By God, these are words that the people of this land do not speak!' The Prophet asked him: 'From which land do you hail, O Addas, and what is your faith?' When Addas replied that he was a Christian from Nineveh, the Prophet smiled gently: 'From the city of the righteous man, Yunus ibn Matta (Jonah, son of Amittai)?' Addas gasped: 'How do you know Yunus?' The Prophet replied: 'He is my brother; he was a prophet, and I am a prophet.' Overcome with awe and spiritual recognition, Addas fell to his knees, kissing the head, hands, and bruised feet of the Messenger of God.
The Choice of Mercy over Vengeance

The report in Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 and Sahih Muslim 1795, from Aishah, is a different scene. When the Prophet returned from Ta'if after Ibn Abd Yalil had refused him, he halted at Qarn al-Tha'alib. A cloud overshadowed him, and Jibril called to him: God had heard what the people had said, and had sent the Angel of the Mountains so that the Prophet might command him as he wished. The hadith does not place this meeting in the vineyard, and it does not use the name Qarn al-Manazil.

بَلْ أَرْجُو أَنْ يُخْرِجَ اللَّهُ مِنْ أَصْلَابِهِمْ مَنْ يَعْبُدُ اللَّهَ وَحْدَهُ لَا يُشْرِكُ بِهِ شَيْئًا
'Rather, I hope that God will bring forth from their loins those who will worship God alone, associating nothing with Him.' — Prophet Muhammad ﷺ (Sahih al-Bukhari & Sahih Muslim)

The Angel of the Mountains greeted him and offered to bring the two great peaks surrounding Makkah—al-Akhshabayn—crashing down upon the transgressors. In that defining moment of supreme spiritual majesty, the Prophet ﷺ chose boundless compassion over retribution, embodying the divine declaration that he was sent solely as a mercy to all creation.
